source_refs.note: Book p. 200-202: 6.5.1 Key Features (vertices to asymptotes) with Figure 6.23, Note on joint equation, rectangular hyperbola, Second definition and Note

items: Vertices: Setting \(y = 0\) in the equation of hyperbola, gives \(x = \pm a\). The points \(A'(-a, 0)\) and \(A(a, 0)\) are the vertices of the hyperbola.
Transverse Axis: The line segment \(A'A\) connecting the vertices is the transverse axis (or focal axis) of the hyperbola. Length of the transverse axis is \(2a\).

Conjugate Axis: A line passes through the centre and perpendicular to the transverse axis is called conjugate axis. Setting \(x = 0\) in the equation of hyperbola, gives \(y^2 = -b^2\), which is impossible, so hyperbola does not meet \(y\)-axis in real points. If we take two points \(B'(0, -b)\) and \(B(0, b)\) on the \(y\)-axis, then the line segment \(B'B\) is called the conjugate axis of the hyperbola. Length of the conjugate axis is \(2b\).
Foci: The foci are at \((\pm c, 0)\), they always lie on the transverse axis. In case of hyperbola \(c^2 = a^2 + b^2\), so that, unlike the ellipse, we may have \(a > b\) or \(a < b\) or \(a = b\).
Centre: The midpoint \(C(0, 0)\) of the segment joining the foci is called the centre of the hyperbola. Note that it is same as the midpoint of the transverse axis.
Symmetry: The equation is unchanged if \(x\) is replaced by \(-x\) and \(y\) by \(-y\); hence the hyperbola is symmetric with respect to both the axis, and the origin.
Eccentricity: The eccentricity \(e\) of a hyperbola is defined as \(e = \frac{c}{a}\). Since \(c > a\), we have \(e > 1\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why does the hyperbola not cut the \(y\)-axis, while the ellipse does? Put \(x = 0\): the ellipse gives \(y^2 = b^2\) (real points \((0, \pm b)\)), the hyperbola gives \(y^2 = -b^2\) (no real point). So for the hyperbola, \(B(0, b)\) and \(B'(0, -b)\) are NOT points of the curve; they are only marked to define the conjugate axis and to help draw the asymptotes.
Why can \(b\) be bigger than \(a\)? In the ellipse \(a\) is the bigger semi-axis. In the hyperbola \(a\) is simply the number under the POSITIVE term, whatever its size; \(c\) is the biggest of the three.

items: Directrices: For the hyperbola \(\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\), there are two directrices given by the vertical lines \(x = \pm\frac{a}{e}\).
Latus Rectum: Each of the focal chords perpendicular to the transverse axis is called a latus rectum (plural: latera recta). The length of each latus rectum is \(\frac{2b^2}{a}\).

Parametric Equations: For all real \(\theta\) such that \(\theta \ne (2n+1)\frac{\pi}{2}\) (where \(n\) is an integer), the point \((a\sec\theta, b\tan\theta)\) lies on the hyperbola \(\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\). Thus, the parametric equations of the hyperbola are: \(x = a\sec\theta\), \(y = b\tan\theta\).

Foci on the \(y\)-axis: If the foci are on the \(y\)-axis at \((0, \pm c)\), the roles of \(x\) and \(y\) are interchanged, and the standard equation becomes \(\frac{y^2}{a^2} - \frac{x^2}{b^2} = 1\), vertices \((0, \pm a)\).
Relation between \(a\), \(b\) and \(e\): Since \(b^2 = c^2 - a^2\), setting \(c = ae\) \(\Rightarrow b^2 = a^2e^2 - a^2 \Rightarrow b^2 = a^2(e^2 - 1)\).

Branches: To analyze the hyperbola further, we write \(\frac{x^2}{a^2} = 1 + \frac{y^2}{b^2} \ge 1\). This shows that \(x^2 \ge a^2\) so \(|x| \ge a\). Therefore, we have \(x \ge a\) or \(x \le -a\). This means that the hyperbola consists of two parts, called its branches. Note that no portion of the curve lies between \(-a < x < a\), because in this interval \(y\) is imaginary.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Where do these come from?
Latus rectum: put \(x = c\) in \(\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\): \(y^2 = b^2\left(\frac{c^2}{a^2} - 1\right) = \frac{b^4}{a^2}\), so \(y = \pm\frac{b^2}{a}\) and the chord has length \(\frac{2b^2}{a}\).
Parametric form: \(\frac{a^2\sec^2\theta}{a^2} - \frac{b^2\tan^2\theta}{b^2} = \sec^2\theta - \tan^2\theta = 1\). The angles \(\theta = (2n+1)\frac{\pi}{2}\) are left out because \(\sec\theta\) and \(\tan\theta\) are undefined there.
Directrices: since \(e > 1\), \(\frac{a}{e} < a\); the directrices lie between the centre and the vertices, inside the gap where there is no curve.

Asymptotes: An important feature of hyperbola that is not shared by ellipses is the presence of asymptotes. An asymptote of a curve \(y = f(x)\) is a line \(y = g(x)\) such that
\[\lim_{x \to \pm\infty}[f(x) - g(x)] = 0\]

For the hyperbola \(\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\), we have \(\frac{y^2}{b^2} = \frac{x^2}{a^2} - 1\) or \(y^2 = \frac{b^2}{a^2}x^2 - b^2\). Notice that
\[\lim_{x \to \pm\infty} \dfrac{y^2}{x^2}\]
\[= \lim_{x \to \pm\infty}\left(\dfrac{b^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{b^2}{x^2}\right)\]
\[= \dfrac{b^2}{a^2}\]

blocks.alt: A hyperbola opening left and right with its two asymptotes y = (b/a)x and y = -(b/a)x crossing at the origin O. Vertices A(a, 0), A'(-a, 0) and foci F(c, 0), F'(-c, 0) are marked on the x-axis; the branches approach the asymptotes.
blocks.caption: Figure 6.23: Hyperbola with its asymptotes y = ±(b/a)x (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.text: That is, as \(x \to \pm\infty\), \(\frac{y^2}{x^2} \to \frac{b^2}{a^2}\), so that \(\frac{y}{x} \to \pm\frac{b}{a}\) and so, \(y = \pm\frac{b}{a}x\) are the (slant) asymptotes as shown in Figure 6.23. The asymptotes of a curve do not meet the curve but distance of any point on the curve from any of the two lines approaches zero.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The book's argument shows the slope of the asymptotes. To see that the gap really goes to zero, take the upper right part \(y = \frac{b}{a}\sqrt{x^2 - a^2}\), \(x > a\):
\[y - \dfrac{b}{a}x = \dfrac{b}{a}\left(\sqrt{x^2 - a^2} - x\right)\]
\[= -\dfrac{b}{a} \cdot \dfrac{a^2}{\sqrt{x^2 - a^2} + x}\]
As \(x \to \infty\) the denominator grows without bound, so the gap tends to 0, but it is never 0 (the curve stays just below the line). This is what 'approaches but never meets' means.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text:
The joint equation of the two asymptotes is
\[\left(y + \dfrac{b}{a}x\right)\left(y - \dfrac{b}{a}x\right) = 0\]
\[y^2 - \dfrac{b^2}{a^2}x^2 = 0\]
\[\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 0\]

Rectangular Hyperbola as a special case: If in \(\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\) the lengths \(a\) and \(b\) become equal then the resulting hyperbola \(x^2 - y^2 = a^2\) is called rectangular hyperbola. In this case asymptotes are perpendicular to each other.
This is obtained by replacing the constant term 1 with 0 in the standard equation.
book_errors: This is obtained by replacing the constant term 1 with 0 in the standard equation.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: This sentence is printed after the rectangular-hyperbola paragraph, but it describes the Note above: the joint equation of the asymptotes \(\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 0\) is obtained by replacing the constant term 1 with 0 in the standard equation. A rectangular hyperbola is obtained by taking \(b = a\), not by replacing 1 with 0.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why are the asymptotes of a rectangular hyperbola perpendicular? With \(b = a\) they are \(y = x\) and \(y = -x\); their slopes are \(1\) and \(-1\), and \(1 \times (-1) = -1\). Its eccentricity is always the same: \(c^2 = a^2 + a^2 = 2a^2\), so \(e = \sqrt{2}\).

The hyperbola can also be defined as, if a point \(P\) moves so that the ratio of its distance from a fixed point \(F\) (the focus) to its distance from a fixed straight line (the directrix) is equal to a constant, \(e\) (greater than 1), the locus of \(P\) is a hyperbola of eccentricity \(e\).
That is, if \(\frac{|PF|}{|PM|} = e\), where \(e > 1\), the locus of \(P\) is a hyperbola.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: The equation of hyperbola can also be derived using the above definition.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Here is that derivation (ours). Take the focus \(F(ae, 0)\) and the directrix \(x = \frac{a}{e}\), with \(e > 1\). For \(P(x, y)\), \(|PF|^2 = e^2|PM|^2\) gives
\[(x - ae)^2 + y^2 = e^2\left(x - \dfrac{a}{e}\right)^2\]
\[x^2 - 2aex + a^2e^2 + y^2\]
\[= e^2x^2 - 2aex + a^2\]
\[x^2(e^2 - 1) - y^2 = a^2(e^2 - 1)\]
\[\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{y^2}{a^2(e^2 - 1)} = 1\]
With \(b^2 = a^2(e^2 - 1)\) this is exactly \(\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\). The same family of curves, the ellipse (\(e < 1\)), parabola (\(e = 1\)) and hyperbola (\(e > 1\)), comes from one focus-directrix rule.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A worked illustration (ours) for \(\frac{x^2}{16} - \frac{y^2}{9} = 1\): \(a = 4\), \(b = 3\), \(c = \sqrt{16 + 9} = 5\).
Vertices \((\pm 4, 0)\); foci \((\pm 5, 0)\); transverse axis length 8; conjugate axis length 6.
\(e = \frac{5}{4}\); directrices \(x = \pm\frac{a}{e} = \pm\frac{16}{5}\); latus rectum \(\frac{2b^2}{a} = \frac{18}{4} = \frac{9}{2}\).
Asymptotes \(y = \pm\frac{3}{4}x\); parametric form \(x = 4\sec\theta\), \(y = 3\tan\theta\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. For \(\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\): vertices \((\pm a, 0)\), foci \((\pm c, 0)\), \(c^2 = a^2 + b^2\).
2. Transverse axis \(2a\), conjugate axis \(2b\); \(a\) may be smaller than \(b\).
3. \(e = \frac{c}{a} > 1\), \(b^2 = a^2(e^2 - 1)\).
4. Directrices \(x = \pm\frac{a}{e}\); latus rectum \(\frac{2b^2}{a}\); parametric \((a\sec\theta, b\tan\theta)\).
5. Asymptotes \(y = \pm\frac{b}{a}x\); joint equation: replace 1 by 0.
6. Rectangular hyperbola: \(a = b\), perpendicular asymptotes, \(e = \sqrt{2}\).
7. Foci on the \(y\)-axis: \(\frac{y^2}{a^2} - \frac{x^2}{b^2} = 1\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Taking \(a\) as the bigger of the two denominators (ellipse habit). For a hyperbola \(a^2\) is under the positive term.
2. Writing the asymptotes as \(y = \pm\frac{a}{b}x\) for \(\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\). Shortcut: replace 1 by 0 and solve for \(y\).
3. Marking \(B(0, \pm b)\) as points on the curve; they are not.
4. Writing the directrices as \(x = \pm ae\) (those are the foci) instead of \(x = \pm\frac{a}{e}\).
5. Using \(e < 1\): a hyperbola always has \(e > 1\).
